questions.question: Identify the defect in the given image:

explanation.text: The given image depicts a newborn with an open neural tube defect, specifically rachischisis or myeloschisis, which is a severe form of spina bifida where the neural tissue is exposed without skin or meningeal covering. Neural tube defects: Category Details Definition Failure of proper closure of neural tube & covering mesoderm/ectoderm; most common congenital CNS anomaly. Inheritance Primary NTDs have multifactorial inheritance.

Maternal risk factors Alcohol, radiation exposure, IDDM, valproate, carbamazepine, zinc and folate deficiency. Types of NTDs Spina bifida occulta, meningocele, encephalocele, myelomeningocele, anencephaly, caudal regression syndrome, dermal sinus, tethered cord, syringomyelia, diastematomyelia, lipoma, iniencephaly.

Spina bifida occulta Midline defect of vertebral bodies without protrusion of spinal cord or meninges; usually asymptomatic and not of consequence. Craniorachischisis Rare malformation with skull and spinal bone defects; brain and nerves exposed; may have other defects like imperforate anus. Meningocele Meninges herniate through vertebral arches or sacrum; spinal cord normal. Fluctuant midline mass that may transilluminate.

Surgery may be delayed in asymptomatic cases with normal neuro findings and skin covering. Myelomeningocele Most common in lumbosacral region; sac-like cystic structure with neural tissue; 80% develop hydrocephalus with type II Chiari malformation. Anencephaly Large defect of calvarium, meninges, and scalp; associated with rudimentary brain due to failure of closure of rostral neuropore.

Iniencephaly Retroflexion of head with occipital and upper spine defects, nearly absent neck; defect can range from acrania to minimal defect. Prenatal diagnosis Detailed ultrasound, MSAFP (maternal serum α-fetoprotein), amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase (AChE). Prevention 0.4 mg folic acid daily for all women of childbearing age; 4 mg daily for high-risk women (prior affected child).

Risk of recurrence 3-4% after 1 affected child; 10% after 2 affected children. Treatment Surgery for defect; VP shunt if hydrocephalus present. Open lesions should be closed within 24 hours. Antibiotics if infection is present.
**Meningoencephalocele (Option B):** Incorrect because a meningoencephalocele is a sac-like protrusion of meninges and brain tissue through a skull defect, typically in the occipital region.
**Occult Spina Bifida (Option C):** Incorrect because occult spina bifida is a closed defect where the vertebral arch fails to fuse, but the skin remains intact,
often presenting with subtle external markers like a tuft of hair or dimple.

**Encephalocele (Option D):** is a rare birth defect that occurs when the neural tube doesn't close completely during fetal development. This results in a sac-like protrusion of brain tissue or membranes through a hole in the skull.

questions.question: The nerve passing through the red arrow marked region has been lesioned. Which of the following will be the clinical presentation?

options.A: Loss of sensation in the mucosa of nasopharynx
options.B: Loss of sensation in maxillary area of face
options.C: Loss of sensation in jaw area
options.D: Loss of sensation in scalp and nose

explanation.text: The superior orbital fissure is a crucial anatomical opening in the skull through which several important nerves pass. These include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), and the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). The ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve provides sensory innervation to the scalp, forehead, upper eyelid, nose, and the mucosa of the frontal sinuses.
If the nerve passing through the superior orbital fissure is lesioned, the patient would experience loss of sensation in the scalp and nose due to the impairment of the ophthalmic nerve (V1).

Incorrect Options: Option A - Loss of sensation in the mucosa of nasopharynx: Incorrect: This sensation is typically provided by branches of the maxillary nerve (V2) and glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not by the ophthalmic nerve (V1), which passes through the superior orbital fissure.

Option B - Loss of sensation in maxillary area of face: Incorrect: The maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve provides sensation to the maxillary region, but it exits the skull through the foramen rotundum, not the superior orbital fissure.

Option C - Loss of sensation in jaw area: Incorrect: The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve provides sensation to the jaw, but it exits through the foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure.

questions.question: Identify the arrow marked nerve:

explanation.text: The medial pectoral nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus and innervates the pectoralis minor and part of the pectoralis major muscles. The nerve typically pierces the pectoralis minor before reaching the pectoralis major. In an anatomical image or dissection, the medial pectoral nerve can be identified as the nerve that passes through or near the pectoralis minor and then continues to supply the pectoralis major.

Incorrect Options: Option B - Lateral Pectoral Nerve: The lateral pectoral nerve arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus and primarily innervates the pectoralis major muscle. Unlike the medial pectoral nerve, it does not pierce the pectoralis minor but rather passes above it. The lateral pectoral nerve is generally found more laterally and superiorly than the medial pectoral nerve.

Option C - Long Thoracic Nerve: The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle. It runs down the side of the thorax and can be seen on the surface of the serratus anterior. It is not associated with the pectoral muscles and is positioned more posteriorly and laterally compared to the pectoral nerves.

Option D - Thoracodorsal Nerve: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and innervates the latissimus dorsi muscle. It is found on the posterior side of the thorax and is not involved with the pectoral muscles, making it distinct from the medial pectoral nerve.

questions.question: Ptosis in horner’s syndrome is due to paralysis of which muscle?

explanation.text: This muscle is a smooth muscle that assists the levator palpebrae superioris in raising the upper eyelid. In Horner's syndrome, there is a disruption of the sympathetic innervation, leading to paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle. This results in a mild ptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid).

Incorrect Options: Option B - Orbitalis: Incorrect: The orbitalis muscle (also known as Müller's muscle) is not directly involved in eyelid movement but is instead associated with the structure of the orbit. It is not the cause of ptosis in Horner's syndrome. Option C - Orbicularis Oculi: Incorrect: The orbicularis oculi muscle is responsible for closing the eyelids and is innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

It is not affected in Horner's syndrome and is not responsible for ptosis. Option D - Sphincter Pupillae: Incorrect: The sphincter pupillae muscle is responsible for constricting the pupil and is innervated by the parasympathetic nervous system. It is not involved in eyelid movement and is not the cause of ptosis in Horner's syndrome.

questions.question: What are the effects of a lesion in Brodmann area 22?

explanation.text: Brodmann area 22, also known as Wernicke's area, is primarily responsible for language comprehension. Lesions in this area lead to difficulties in understanding spoken and written language, resulting in receptive aphasia. Patients with this condition can speak fluently but often produce nonsensical sentences and have trouble understanding others.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Expressive aphasia: This is typically associated with damage to Brodmann area 44 and 45 (Broca's area) rather than Brodmann area 22. Expressive aphasia affects speech production, making it difficult for the patient to form

grammatically correct sentences. Option C - Poor repetition of language: Poor repetition of language is often linked to damage in the arcuate fasciculus, which connects Wernicke's area and Broca's area, rather than directly to Brodmann area 22. Option D - Poor naming: Poor naming is often associated with damage to areas involved in language processing and retrieval, such as the left temporal lobe, but not specifically with Brodmann area 22 alone.

questions.question: A patient with loss of sensation on lateral 3 1 / 2 hand and thenar atrophy. Which nerve is involved?

explanation.text: Lateral 3½ fingers (thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of ring finger) on the palmar side are supplied sensory-wise by the median nerve. Thenar atrophy suggests motor loss to thenar muscles, which are innervated by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. These two features together are classic for median nerve injury, typically at the wrist (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome) or more proximally.

Nerves of the hand: Nerve Motor Dysfunction Sensory Dysfunction Common Deformity/Condition Median Nerve Weakness of thenar muscles (thumb opposition), flexor muscles of forearm Loss of sensation in lateral 3.5 fingers (thumb, index, middle, half of the ring finger) Ape hand (thenar atrophy), Carpal tunnel syndrome Ulnar Nerve (Option B ruled out) Weakness of intrinsic hand muscles (especially interossei), hypothenar muscles Loss of sensation in medial 1.5 fingers (little and half of the ring finger) Claw hand, Hypothenar atrophy, Cubital tunnel syndrome Radial Nerve (Option C ruled out) Inability to extend wrist and fingers (wrist drop) Loss of sensation over the dorsum of the hand Wrist drop, Saturday night palsy, Radial tunnel syndrome Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN) (Option D ruled out) Inability to flex thumb and index finger (loss of flexion of distal phalanges) No sensory loss (pure motor neuropathy) Inability to make "OK" sign (difficulty flexing thumb and index finger) Long Thoracic Nerve Weakness of serratus anterior muscle, affecting scapular movement No sensory loss Winged scapula (scapula protrudes from the back).

questions.question: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness during daily activities. On examination, she is unable to make an 'O' shape by opposing her thumb and index finger. Which of the following muscles is most likely involved?

explanation.text: The patient’s inability to make an 'O' shape with the thumb and index finger (tip-to-tip pinch) is a classical sign of anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome, which is a pure motor branch of the median nerve.

The AIN innervates deep forearm muscles, specifically: Flexor pollicis longus Lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus Pronator quadratus Hence, the actual motor deficit is due to involvement of FPL and FDP to the index, not due to abductor pollicis brevis or any thenar muscle. However, none of the muscles directly innervated by AIN are listed in the options.

Among the choices, the only muscle purely and entirely innervated by the median nerve is abductor pollicis brevis, making it the most appropriate answer based on: The nerve implicated (median), The pattern of weakness, And the available options.

Muscles of the Palm: Functions and Innervations Muscle Group Muscles Function Innervation Thenar muscles • Abductor pollicis brevis • Flexor pollicis brevis • Opponens pollicis • Abducts thumb • Flexes thumb • Opposes thumb AbPB: Median nerve (recurrent branch) FPB: Dual (Median + Ulnar) OP: Median (variable) Hypothenar muscles • Abductor digiti minimi • Flexor digiti minimi brevis • Opponens digiti minimi Controls movement of little finger Ulnar nerve (deep branch) Lumbricals • 1st & 2nd (lateral) • 3rd & 4th (medial) Flex MCPs and extend IP joints Lateral 2: Median nerve Medial 2: Ulnar nerve Palmar interossei • Three muscles (unipennate) Adduction of fingers (PAD) Ulnar nerve (deep branch) Dorsal interossei • Four muscles (bipennate) Abduction of fingers (DAB) Ulnar nerve (deep branch) Adductor pollicis • Oblique and transverse heads Adducts the thumb Ulnar nerve (deep branch) Palmaris brevis • One small superficial muscle Tenses skin over hypothenar eminence Ulnar nerve (superficial branch) Opponens pollicis (Option A): Incorrect because it is mainly innervated by the median nerve, but may receive a contribution from the ulnar nerve (dual innervation).
Also, it is responsible for thumb opposition, not for the tip-to-tip pinch affected in AIN palsy.
**Flexor pollicis brevis (Option C):** Incorrect. It has dual innervation (superficial head by median, deep head by ulnar). Not purely median.
**Palmar interossei (Option D):** Incorrect. These are ulnar nerve -innervated muscles, unrelated to thumb-index pinch or median nerve pathology.

questions.question: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to which cranial nerve?

explanation.text: Cranial Nerves IX (Glossopharyngeal) and X (Vagus): The gag reflex involves both sensory and motor components. The sensory component of the gag reflex is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), which detects the stimulus at the back of the throat. The motor

component is controlled by the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X), which causes the muscles in the throat to contract. Injury to either of these nerves can result in an absent gag reflex. Incorrect Options: Option B - 10 and 7: While cranial nerve X (vagus) is involved in the gag reflex, cranial nerve VII (facial nerve) is not. The facial nerve primarily controls muscles of facial expression, not the gag reflex.

Option C - 7 and 5: Incorrect: Cranial nerve V (trigeminal) provides sensation to the face and motor control for mastication, and cranial nerve VII controls facial expression. Neither of these nerves is involved in the gag reflex. Option D - 5 and 9: While cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal) is involved in the gag reflex, cranial nerve V (trigeminal) is not. The trigeminal nerve is responsible for facial sensation and chewing.

questions.question: Identify the marked structure:

explanation.text: Internal Capsule The internal capsule is a compact bundle of projection fibres that connects the cerebral cortex with subcortical centres such as the thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord. It contains both afferent (sensory) fibres from the thalamus to the cortex and efferent (motor) fibres from the cortex to the cerebral peduncle and midbrain.

INTERNAL CAPSULE: V-shaped projection fiber—angled laterally, present between thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. Parts of Internal Capsule: Anterior limb: Between caudate nucleus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. Posterior limb: Between thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. Genu: Between anterior and posterior limb. Sublentiform: Present below the lentiform.

Retrolentiform: Present behind lentiform. Lesion of Internal Capsule Occurs due to hemorrhage, leading to spastic paralysis (due to involvement of pyramidal and extrapyramidal fibers for the upper limb, trunk, and lower limb) and loss of sensations in the opposite half of the body. Most commonly involved artery – Charcot’s artery of cerebral hemorrhage (striate branches from middle cerebral artery).
Lesions in the sublentiform and retrolentiform parts of the internal capsule lead to visual loss and auditory defects. (Option B, C, and D ruled out)

explanation.text: The occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery causes lateral medullary syndrome also called the Wallenberg syndrome. Wallenberg syndrome: Also known as Lateral medullary syndrome Pathology:
Blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. It supplies areas behind the inferior olivary nucleus. Damage to the lateral segment of the medulla posterior to the inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.question: A 32-year-old patient presents with a swelling below the ear and complains of pain in the lobule of the ear. The patient also reports difficulty in completely closing the left eye and experiences trouble while eating food. What nerve is most likely to be damaged in this case?

explanation.text: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) controls facial expressions, including eye closure and smiling. Damage to it can cause weakness or paralysis in these muscles. Additionally, it regulates muscles for eating and swallowing, which aligns with the patient's eating difficulties.

External Ear consists of two main parts: Pinna (Auricle) External Auditory Meatus Aspects Auricle (Pinna) External Auditory Meatus Composition Elastic cartilage, except lobule (fibrofatty tissue) Cartilaginous part (Outer 1/3) with hair and ceruminous glands Bony part (Inner 2/3), with thin skin continuous with the tympanic membrane, lacks hair and glands.

Parts Concha (Depression leading to the external meatus) Helix (Prominent rim with anterior and posterior limbs) Antihelix (Parallel ridge to the helix) Tragus & Antitragus (Separated by inter-tragic notch) Cymba Conchae (Above crus of helix) Lobule (Soft, fleshy part below antitragus) Nerve Supply Lateral Surface Lower third: Great auricular nerve (C2, C3) Upper two-thirds: Auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3) Concha: Auricular branch of vagus (CN X) (Alderman’s Nerve) Medial Surface Lower third: Great auricular nerve Upper two-thirds: Lesser occipital nerve (C2) Roof & Anterior Wall: Auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3) Floor & Posterior Wall: Auricular branch of vagus (CN X) Clinical Relevance McEwen’s triangle (Cymba Conchae) It is a surgical landmark on the temporal bone to locate the mastoid antrum.

**Furuncles (cartilaginous part) susceptible to infections Greater Auricular nerve (Option A):** Damage to this nerve might result in altered sensation around the ear, but it wouldn't explain the symptoms mentioned in the case.
**Auriculotemporal nerve (Option B):** provides sensation to the external ear and part of the scalp. However, it doesn't control facial movement, eye closure, or eating functions.

**Vagus nerve (Option D):** While damage to the vagus nerve might cause some difficulties in swallowing and speech, it would not explain the specific symptoms of facial muscle weakness, inability to close the eye, or earlobe pain described in the case.

questions.question: Which structure is not present in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?

explanation.text: The tail of the caudate nucleus is not present in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. The caudate nucleus is part of the basal ganglia and its tail arches around and terminates in the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hippocampus: The hippocampus is present in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

It is a key structure involved in memory and spatial navigation. Option C - Fimbriae: The fimbriae of the hippocampus are present in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. They are bundles of axons that emerge from the hippocampus and converge to form the fornix.

Option D - Collateral eminence: The collateral eminence is a ridge on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle caused by the underlying collateral sulcus. It is indeed present in the floor of the inferior horn.

questions.question: What is the vertebral level shown by the arrow in the image?

explanation.text: If the blue line is at the L4-L5 level, then this option is correct. L4-L5 refers to the intervertebral space between the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4) and the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5). This is a common area for vertebral numbering and is often used as a reference point in medical and anatomical contexts.

**L2-L3 (Option A):** This option is incorrect as the blue line is at the L4-L5 level. The L2-L3 level would be higher up on the spine, and if the blue line is visibly at L4-L5, then this option is not the correct answer.

**L5-S1 (Option C):** This option is incorrect as the blue line is at the L4-L5 level. L5-S1 refers to the intervertebral space between the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and the first sacral vertebra (S1), which is lower down the spine. If the blue line is at L4-L5, then this option is not the correct answer.

**L3-L4 (Option D):** This option is incorrect as the blue line is at the L4-L5 level. L3-L4 refers to the intervertebral space between the third lumbar vertebra (L3) and the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4). If the blue line is visible at the L4-L5 level, then this option is not the correct answer.

questions.question: The patient presented with ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the face, Horner's syndrome, and Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the body. Which artery is involved in the syndrome based on clinical features?

explanation.text: The patient's presentation with ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the face, Horner's syndrome, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the body is suggestive lateral medullary syndrome also called the Wallenberg syndrome. The occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery causes lateral medullary syndrome also called the Wallenberg syndrome.

Wallenberg syndrome: Also known as Lateral medullary syndrome Pathology: Blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. It supplies areas behind the inferior olivary nucleus. Damage to the lateral segment of the medulla posterior to the inferior olivary nucleus.

Clinical manifestation: Anatomical location Presenting clinical feature Nucleus ambiguous gives fibers to IX, X, and XI cranial nerves Ipsilateral paralysis of muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx Spinal nucleus and spinal tract of the trigeminal nerve Ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss Lateral spinothalamic tract Contralateral body pain and temperature loss Vestibular nuclei Vertigo Inferior cerebellar peduncle, spino cerebellar tracts, and part of cerebellum Ipsilateral ataxia Sympathetic fibres descend from the hypothalamus to cells in the lateral horn of spinal cord Horner’s syndrome, comprising ptosis, enophthalmos, miosis, and anhydrosis Superior cerebellar artery (Option B): The superior cerebellar artery primarily supplies the superior portion of the cerebellum and parts of the midbrain.

While it can lead to symptoms like ataxia or vertigo, it doesn’t typically cause the specific signs described (ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the face, Horner's syndrome, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature in the body).

**Basilar artery (Option C):** NA blockage in the basilar artery can lead to locked-in syndrome or other pontine deficits Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) (Option D): AICA strokes can cause symptoms like vertigo, ataxia, and facial weakness.

explanation.text: The highlighted structure is the inferior cerebellar peduncle, a white matter bundle linking the medulla oblongata to the cerebellum. It is mainly supplied by the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA), a branch of the vertebral artery.

Blood supply of various parts of brain: Structure Blood Supply Medulla Anterior spinal artery Posterior spinal artery Posterior inferior cerebellar artery Medullary branch from basilar artery Pons Anterior inferior cerebellar artery Pontine branch from basilar artery Superior cerebellar artery Midbrain Posterior cerebral artery Superior cerebellar artery Thalamus Posterior communicating artery Posterior cerebral artery Cerebellum Posterior inferior cerebellar artery Anterior inferior cerebellar artery Superior cerebellar artery Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (Option B): The anterior inferior cerebral artery (AICA) a branch of the basilar artery, supplies blood to the anteroinferior cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncle, and inferolateral pons.

questions.question: Which of the following structures is derived from the marked point in the given image?

explanation.text: Structures derived from the paraxial mesoderm include the somites. Somites are bilaterally paired blocks of mesoderm that form on either side of the neural tube during early embryonic development. The somites give rise to various structures in the embryo, including the axial skeleton (such as vertebrae), skeletal muscles, and the dermis of the skin.

Intraembryonic Mesoderm/ Secondary Mesoderm: Formed by the proliferation of cells from the primitive streak. Separates the ectoderm and endoderm except in specific regions that remain bilaminar throughout life: Prochordal plate (future oral cavity) Cloacal membrane (future anal and urogenital openings) Midline caudal to the prochordal plate Formation of intraembryonic mesoderm. (B) is a section along axis in (A) Subdivisions: 1.

Paraxial Mesoderm 2. Lateral Plate Mesoderm 3. Intermediate Mesoderm Located on either side of the notochord and becomes thick. It forms a thinner layer located laterally. A longitudinal strip found between the paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm. It forms: Somitomeres: Form mesoderm and muscles of the head and jaw. Somites: Form midline axial skeleton, skeletal muscles and dermis of back.

It forms: Somatopleuric (parietal) layer: Forms connective tissue of the body wall and limbs, such as appendicular skeleton bones, muscles and dermis of periphery. Splanchnopleuric (visceral) layers: Forms connective tissue and smooth muscle layers of the gut, cardiac muscle and the circulatory system. It forms: Urinary and genital systems.

Somites: Paraxial mesoderm becomes segmented to form 42-44 pairs of somites develop on either side of the neural tube and notochord. Appear between the 20th and 30th day, marking the 4th week as the somite period. Somite Structure: Sclerotome: Ventromedial part; forms vertebral column and ribs. Dermatome: Lateral part; forms dermis of skin and subcutaneous tissue. Myotome: Intermediate part; forms striated muscle.
**Kidneys (Option B):** Kidneys are the derivatives of the intermediate mesoderm.
**Dorsal root ganglion (Option C):** Dorsal root ganglia are derived from the neural crest cells.
**Parietal pleura (Option D):** The pericardial, pleural, and peritoneal cavities, housing vital organs, originate from the lateral plate mesoderm during embryonic development.

questions.question: The marked structure relays efferents to which nucleus of the thalamus? [

explanation.text: The marked structure is the fornix. Fornix is the major efferent tract of the hippocampus. The fornix sends efferents to the mammillary bodies, and the mammillothalamic tract connects the mammillary bodies to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. This pathway is part of the Papez circuit, involved in memory and emotional processing.

Thalamic Nuclei and their Connection: Anterior nucleus Receives input from hypothalamic mammillary nuclei via mammillothalamic tract. Receives input from the hippocampus via fornix. Projects fibers to the cingulate gyrus. Dorsomedial nucleus Part of the limbic system. Lesion results in memory loss (Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome). Intralaminar nuclei Receives input from the reticular formation. Projects fibers to the neocortex.
Sends fibers to other thalamic nuclei (unlike other thalamic nuclei, which project to different

cortical areas). Dorsal tier nucleus Lateral dorsal nucleus: Posterior extension of the anterior nucleus. Pulvinar: Largest thalamic nucleus. Receives input from the lateral and medial geniculate bodies. Integrates visual and auditory input. Ventral tier nucleus Ventral anterior nucleus: Receives input from globus pallidus and substantia nigra. Projects fibers to the motor cortex.

Ventral posterior nucleus: Contains three subnuclei: Ventral posterolateral (VPL): Receives input from spinothalamic tracts and medial lemniscus. Ventral posteromedial (VPM): Receives input from trigeminothalamic tracts. Ventral posterior inferior (VPI): Receives input from vestibular nuclei.
**Lateral nucleus of thalamus (Option B):** The lateral nucleus functions as the hunger center, promoting eating when stimulated, while its destruction leads to starvation.

**Ventro-postero-lateral nucleus of thalamus (Option C):** The ventro-postero-lateral nucleus of the thalamus processes sensations like pain, vibration, proprioception, and light touch from the spinothalamic tract and dorsal column pathways.

**Posterior nucleus of the thalamus (Option D):** The posterior nucleus aids in thermoregulation by promoting heat conservation. It triggers the sympathetic nervous system, causing peripheral vasoconstriction to retain heat.

balance Sensory Glossopharyngeal IX Taste and sensation from posterior 1/3 of tongue, swallowing, salivation (parotid gland), monitoring carotid body and sinus chemo- and baroreceptors, elevation of pharynx/larynx (stylopharyngeus) Both Vagus X Taste from supraglottic region, swallowing, soft palate elevation, midline uvula, talking, cough reflex, parasympathetics to thoracoabdominal viscera, monitoring aortic arch chemo- and baroreceptors Both Accessory XI Head turning, shoulder shrugging (SCM, trapezius) Motor Hypoglossal XII Tongue movement Motor
